sentences.text: Tonsala hildegardae was a large, flightless seabird comparable in size to a great penguin and larger than its relative Plotopterum.
The bird was heavily adapted for swimming and diving, featuring paddle-shaped wings and a scapula with a thin, expanded blade similar to penguins to aid propulsion.
The wing structure of Tonsala, particularly the humerus and radius, shows convergent evolution resembling early penguins and flightless auks rather than its related Pelecaniformes.
The ulna of Tonsala shares similarities with the unrelated Paleocene penguin Waimanu.
The pelvis of Tonsala was broad, shallow, and elongated with a praeacetabular portion twice the size of the postacetabular portion, resembling the pelvis of modern darters.
The caudal vertebrae of Tonsala were large, twice the size of those found in the modern great cormorant.

The complete beak of Tonsala was presumably proportionally longer than modern relatives and featured elongated, very narrow nostrils, unlike modern Suloids which have greatly reduced or absent nostrils.
The skull of Tonsala was devoid of a vomer bone.
The species name hildegardae was given to honor Hildegarde Howard, the American paleontologist who described Plotopterum.
Cow shark teeth found with Tonsala fossils suggest that sharks fed on the carcasses of these birds.
The type species Tonsala hildegardae was formally described in 1980 by Storrs L. Olson based on fossils collected by Douglas Emlong from the Pysht Formation on the Olympic Peninsula.
In 1979, Storrs L. Olson and Hasegawa Yoshikazu identified fossils from Washington and Japan as a distinct genus within the family Plotopteridae.
A new species, Tonsala buchanani, was proposed in 2011 based on Oligocene fossils from the Pysht and Makah Formations.
Remains from Japan that were tentatively assigned to a new Tonsala species in 1996 were redescribed in 2019 as a new genus and species, Stenornis kanmonensis.

In 2016, Mayr and Goedert referred specimens from the Late Eocene to Early Oligocene of the Jansen Creek Member of the Makah Formation to Tonsala, including a partial pelvis tentatively assigned to T. hildegardae and a coracoid tentatively referred as ?Tonsala sp.
In 2017, a partial skeleton of T. hildegardae containing the first known tarsometatarsus for the genus was referred to Tonsala by Mayr and Goedert.
There are four recorded fossil occurrences of Tonsala in the Paleobiology Database.
Tonsala likely propelled itself in water using wing upstroke movements with a force comparable to modern penguins.
The enlarged patella in Tonsala suggests it stood upright on land like modern penguins and cormorants.
Tonsala was first described by Olson in 1980 as a member of the clade Sulae.
In 2017, Mayr and Goedert proposed the clade Tonsalinae to include Tonsala and other large plotopterids.
Within the clade Tonsalinae, Tonsala is considered the most basal member.
In 2017, Mayr and Goedert established the clade Tonsalinae with Tonsala as the type genus, including derived plotopterids except for Phocavis, Stemec, and Plotopterum.
In 2021, the species Tonsala buchanani was transferred to the genus Klallamornis, where it became the type species.
Fossils of Tonsala are found in Late Oligocene terrains in the State of Washington and Japan.
Tonsala lived between 33.9 and 23.04 million years ago, during the Rupelian to Chattian stages.
Tonsala was one of the smallest and most common plotopterids living along the Pacific Northwest coast during the Oligocene.
It has been suggested that Phocavis maritimus may be synonymous with Tonsala hildegardae.
Following criticism of Dyke et al. (2016), Mayr and Goedert tentatively referred one partial skeleton previously assigned to the type species as cf. Tonsala hildegardae.
The exact phylogenetic relationships of plotopterids, including Tonsala, with modern bird taxa remain debated.
In 2004, Gerald Mayr hypothesized that plotopterids were the sister group to modern penguins, a theory that has since been heavily criticized.
